summary:
The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, provides funding for multiple federal departments and agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2024, using money from the Treasury not otherwise appropriated. The Act is organized into seven divisions (A through G), each addressing different areas of government. Beyond setting spending levels, the Act imposes numerous policy conditions and restrictions on the use of those funds.

Division A funds military construction, veterans affairs, and related agencies. Its general provisions limit the availability of appropriations to the current fiscal year unless expressly extended, prohibit funding for any project known to violate federal risk-assessment, property-rights, or unfunded-mandate laws, and bar the naming of any project for a sitting member of the House. Reports required by the division generally must go to the relevant House and Senate appropriations subcommittees. The division also prohibits funds from being used for first-class travel contrary to federal regulations, for contracts with employers that have not complied with Executive Order 12989 on immigration verification, or for network systems that do not block pornography—though this last prohibition does not hinder law-enforcement investigations. On detainee policy, no funds in the Act may be used to construct, renovate, or expand any U.S. facility to house individuals detained at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, as of June 24, 2009, who are not U.S. citizens or service members, apart from modifications at the naval station itself. Further, the VA is restricted from reporting a person as “adjudicated as a mental defective” for firearm-disqualification purposes solely under certain statutory procedures.

Division C covers Commerce, Justice, Science, and related agencies. It includes a series of firearms and trade provisions. No funds may be used to require an export license for most firearm parts, accessories, or attachments being shipped to Canada if the wholesale value does not exceed $500, provided the exporter files the needed declarations and does not export fully automatic weapons, or barrels, cylinders, or receivers, except for official use by Canadian federal, provincial, or municipal governments. The President may temporarily require licenses if finding that Canada’s import controls are inadequate and cause significant diversion for terrorism or conflict escalation, but only after publishing that determination in the Federal Register. The Act forbids using funds to deny the importation of certain U.S.-origin “curios or relics” firearms, parts, or ammunition that otherwise qualify, and likewise bars denial of a shotgun import application simply for lacking a sporting purpose if the same model in the same configuration was not denied on that ground before January 1, 2011. Implementation of the Arms Trade Treaty is prohibited until the Senate provides its advice and consent to ratification. Additionally, no funds may be used to transfer or release Khalid Sheikh Mohammed or other detainees held at Guantánamo on or after June 24, 2009, into the United States, its territories, or possessions. The division also rescinds certain remaining unobligated balances from the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative previously provided in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, and reappropriates equivalent amounts on September 30, 2024, for the same purposes, designating them as emergency requirements.

Division G, “Other Matters,” includes the Compact of Free Association Amendments Act of 2024, which amends Title 38 of the U.S. Code to authorize the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to provide hospital care and medical services to veterans residing in the Freely Associated States—the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, and the Republic of Palau—so long as each remains a party to its respective compact. Division G also amends Title XIX of the Social Security Act (Medicaid), though the specific changes are not detailed in these notes.

Across all divisions, every amount designated by Congress as an emergency requirement under the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act becomes available only if the President subsequently designates all such amounts as emergency requirements and transmits those designations to Congress. The explanatory statement printed in the Senate Congressional Record around March 5, 2024, and submitted by the Senate Appropriations Committee chair, is given the force of a joint conference committee statement for allocating and implementing the funds in Divisions A through F.
